A 23-year-old Pakistani woman presented with a 2-month history of recurrent blackouts, blurring of vision, and moderate frontal headaches radiating to the whole head, associated with vertigo, dizziness, palpitations, and postural weakness. She had been diagnosed with epilepsy 2 months earlier and was taking antiepileptic medication.  

On examination, pulses in both upper limbs were deficient and blood pressure could not be measured. She was anemic, and a bruit was audible over the left subclavian fossa. Fundoscopy showed optic-disk cupping with irregular margins in the right eye; the left eye was normal. Respiratory, neurologic, and psychiatric evaluations were unremarkable.  

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin 10 g/dL, platelet count 494 000/mL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 35 mm/hr. Red-cell indices showed microcytosis (MCV 58.7 fL) and hypochromasia (MCH 19.2 pg). Serum ferritin was elevated at 315.5 ng/mL. Hemoglobin electrophoresis demonstrated hemoglobin A₂ 4.7%. Liver tests were abnormal (direct bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL; ALT 152 U/L; ALP 317 U/L), and C-reactive protein was positive. Serum iron, total iron-binding capacity, transferrin, antinuclear antibodies, electrocardiogram, echocardiogram, and electroencephalogram were normal.  

A computed tomography angiogram of the chest showed a normal ascending and descending aorta and aortic arch, but diffuse intimal thickening with narrowing at the origins of the brachiocephalic, right common carotid, and left subclavian arteries, with extensive collateral circulation in the neck, chest, and axillae.

A 9-month-old spayed female Ragdoll cat was evaluated for 5 days of persistent vomiting and one episode of hematemesis, along with reduced appetite and lethargy. The cat’s history was unremarkable; it had been fed a raw rabbit–based raw food (BARF) diet for 3 months. On examination, the cat was moderately dehydrated (≈7%), febrile (39.9°C), with pale mucous membranes (capillary refill time ~3 s) and mild discomfort on abdominal palpation; body condition score was 4/9 (4.2 kg). Complete blood count, serum biochemistry, and FIV/FeLV tests were within normal limits or negative. Thoracic and abdominal radiographs were unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasound revealed multiple rounded, echogenic neoformations at the pyloric antrum and mild mesenteric lymphadenomegaly; the remainder of the abdomen appeared normal. Intravenous fluids and omeprazole were initiated. Endoscopy showed several sessile, smooth-surfaced nodules (0.5–2 cm) in the pyloric antrum; the duodenum was normal. Cytological brushing of the gastric mucosa demonstrated mucosal cells, mixed neutrophilic and macrophagic inflammation, and occasional large, non-septate hyphae with irregular diameter and branching. Pending histology, the cat was treated with fluids, omeprazole, maropitant, sucralfate, and ketoconazole (20 mg/kg q12h).

A 53-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and bipolar disorder was admitted for a 4-week history of progressive asthenia, anorexia, and a 7-kg weight loss, with vomiting during the last 2 days. On examination, her BMI was 18.2 kg/m2 and she was obnubilated; the ECG was normal. Laboratory studies showed:  
• Serum calcium 3.8 mmol/L (normal phosphorus), nonregenerative normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 9 g/dL), and acute functional renal failure (creatinine clearance 30 mL/min).  
• PTH 9 ng/L.  
• Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia; negative 24-hour proteinuria; no monoclonal peak on serum or urine immunoelectrophoresis; normal serum free light-chain ratio.  

She received IV saline and one dose of zoledronate, with normalization of calcium and renal function by day 3. A CT scan of the body showed two osteolytic lesions of the left frontal and temporal skull bones, multiple hypodense micronodules in all hepatic segments, and multiple splenic nodules. Brain MRI demonstrated T2-hyperintense, T1-isointense, gadolinium-enhancing lesions in the same skull regions. A DEXA scan revealed osteopenia (lumbar spine T-score –2.4). Mammography, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal. Bone marrow biopsy and labial salivary gland histology were unremarkable. A percutaneous fine-needle aspiration of the liver showed noncaseating granulomatous hepatitis without malignancy. The intradermal tuberculin test was negative. During this period, hypercalcemia recurred, and two additional doses of zoledronate were administered 15 days apart despite initial correction.

A female infant was delivered at 26 weeks and 6 days of gestation to a healthy 26-year-old primigravida mother after an uneventful pregnancy until 19 weeks, when routine ultrasound identified a 34×28 mm sacrococcygeal mass with internal and external components. Amniocentesis showed a normal array comparative genomic hybridization, and a fetal echocardiogram was normal. At 22 weeks, MRI demonstrated a 60×70×57 mm sacrococcygeal mass with mixed features—predominantly solid with a 40 mm cyst—and no invasion or compression of pelvic structures or the coccyx (Altman type II). Subsequent ultrasounds showed rapid growth to 80×60 mm with profuse vascularization.

Spontaneous vaginal delivery occurred after antenatal steroids. The infant’s birth weight was 1300 g, and Apgar scores were 0, 0, and 5 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes. She required positive-pressure ventilation with FiO₂ up to 1.0 and intravenous adrenaline, with return of heart rate after 6 minutes. A single dose of surfactant was administered.

On admission to the NICU, vital signs were: heart rate 103/min, respiratory rate 70/min, blood pressure 19/15 mm Hg (mean 17), and axillary temperature 34.1 °C. She was ventilated on SIMV with volume guarantee (PIP 25 cm H₂O, PEEP 5 cm H₂O, rate 70/min, FiO₂ 1.0, VG 6 mL/kg). Physical examination revealed pallor, prolonged capillary refill, and a 14×7×4 cm, approximately 750 g, reddish sacrococcygeal mass with visible active bleeding. Initial management included repeated saline and glucose boluses, transfusion of red blood cells (30 mL/kg), fresh-frozen plasma (10 mL/kg), and platelets (10 mL/kg). Post-transfusion hemoglobin remained 5.8 g/dL. Severe metabolic acidosis was noted (pH 6.80, HCO₃⁻ 8.6 mmol/L, base excess −25).

An 89-year-old woman with persistent atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) and hypertension presented with acute speech disturbance and right-sided weakness. On examination she was alert, had global aphasia, right facial asymmetry, right upper- and lower-limb paresis with decreased tone, and a right Babinski sign; NIH Stroke Scale score was 19. She had no history of COVID-19, and two mRNA vaccine doses; RT-PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 on admission and hospital day 3 was negative. 

Noncontrast head CT showed early ischemic changes in the left insula and frontal lobe. CT angiography revealed acute occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery at M1/M2 and chronic occlusion of the left internal carotid artery; an incidental mass in the left orbit was also noted. She received intravenous thrombolysis with reperfusion of the left ICA. Conventional angiography confirmed left MCA occlusion and restored flow in the ICA and ACA. Mechanical thrombectomy achieved angiographic reperfusion of the MCA but no clinical improvement; follow-up CT confirmed an infarct in the left MCA territory. 

Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral oval lesions in the medial orbits, which were initially interpreted as orbital tumors. CT angiography of the chest showed pulmonary emboli in segmental arteries of the right lower lobe. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, degenerative mitral and aortic valves, and severe low-gradient aortic stenosis with preserved ejection fraction. Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring confirmed atrial fibrillation; ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was normal. 

Laboratory studies showed elevated C-reactive protein (10.74 mg/dL) and procalcitonin (0.11 ng/mL) with normal renal, liver function, and electrolytes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild pleocytosis (10 cells/µL) and elevated protein (55 mg/dL) with normal glucose. Multiple blood and urine cultures were negative, and repeat SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative. Vasculitic, autoimmune, viral infection, and malignancy screens were unremarkable, and rheumatology and angiology consultations excluded systemic vasculitis, neoplasm, and histiocytosis.

clinical_record:
A 35-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder and chronic joint pain presented with a 15-month history of swelling and redness of her hands. She reported no precipitating factors, including temperature changes. She had occupational exposure to pool chemicals but noted no improvement with glove use. She described chronic joint pain in her hands and back. Prior treatments with topical mupirocin and emollients were unsuccessful. She denied coagulopathy but endorsed a 4-year history of injecting heroin, buprenorphine, suboxone, and morphine without tourniquet use into multiple sites, including the dorsal hands, wrists, and forearms. Three years after cessation of intravenous drug use, she experienced intermittent, painless, symmetric swelling of both hands. Two years later, during the second trimester of pregnancy, she developed persistent hand and foot edema with new erythema and was hospitalized for cardiac and thrombosis evaluation. An echocardiogram showed a normal ejection fraction; no diagnosis was made. Eleven months postpartum, examination revealed bilateral dorsal hand erythema and edema sharply demarcated at the wrists. Punch biopsy showed small‐vessel ectasia and minimal perivascular lymphocytes. Laboratory studies demonstrated negative antinuclear antibody, extractable nuclear antigen panel, and rheumatoid factor. Creatine kinase and aldolase were mildly elevated. Six-month–old creatinine levels, hepatic function tests, and hepatitis panels were normal.

A 40-year-old man presented with a painful nodule on the lower part of his right leg. He reported that the lesion had been stable in size and painless for 4 years but had enlarged and become tender over the past 6 months. There was no history of trauma or personal or family history of malignancy.

On examination, an irregular, firm, erythematous, mobile, tender mass measuring 3.5 × 2.3 × 1.7 cm was noted just above the lateral malleolus of the right leg. No popliteal or inguinal lymphadenopathy was present, and there were no other suspicious cutaneous lesions. Routine blood tests, including complete blood count, fasting blood sugar, liver and renal function tests, were within normal limits. Tests for hepatitis B surface antigen and HIV were negative.

The patient underwent a local excision. Grossly, there was a lobulated, tan-gray, firm mass partly covered by skin, measuring 3.5 × 2.3 × 1.7 cm. On light microscopy, the dermal tumor extended into the superficial subcutis and was composed of nests and fascicles of spindle-shaped to epithelioid cells with pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and prominent nucleoli within a collagenous stroma. Mitotic figures, including atypical forms, measured 7–8 per 10 high-power fields. There was no intracytoplasmic melanin pigment, and the overlying epidermis showed no increase in basal melanocytes, junctional activity, or pagetoid spread.

Immunohistochemical staining showed strong positivity for vimentin and focal positivity for Melan-A and HMB-45. The tumor cells were negative for S-100 protein, pancytokeratin, epithelial membrane antigen, and CD31.

The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated peripheral rim enhancement, causing severe foraminal stenosis without attachment to pelvic organs. clinical_record:
A 65-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia presented for urologic evaluation. His prostate-specific antigen level was 0.796 ng/mL. Uroflowmetry revealed reduced urine flow, prolonged micturition time, and obstructive findings. He was started on oral Alfuzosin 10 mg once daily. On day 9 of therapy, he reported loss of appetite and malaise, followed by generalized pruritus, dark urine, and jaundice. He denied use of aspirin, acetaminophen, or herbal medicines and had no history of liver disease. On examination, he was jaundiced but had no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory studies showed leukocyte count 5.8 K/μL, AST 175 U/L (0–40), ALT 402 U/L (0–55), alkaline phosphatase 235 U/L (15–250), γ-glutamyl transferase 327 U/L (8–61), total bilirubin 7.6 mg/dL (0.2–1.2), and direct bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL (0–0.25). Abdominal ultrasonography showed normal liver, gallbladder, common bile duct, and intrahepatic bile ducts. Serologic tests for HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, anti-HCV, anti-HAV IgM, anti-HEV, HEV RNA, and HCV RNA were negative. Autoimmune markers (ANA, AMA, ASMA, LKM-1) were negative. Metabolic evaluations—including transferrin saturation, ferritin, alpha-1 antitrypsin, ceruloplasmin, 24-hour urinary copper, and ophthalmologic exam for Kayser–Fleischer rings—were normal. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated a normal biliary anatomy.

clinical_record:
A 74-year-old man with a history of metastatic prostate cancer and a known left upper lobe lung mass presented with four weeks of progressive vertigo, described as the sensation that “the floor was wobbling” and “the room was swaying,” leading to difficulty ambulating. A few days before admission, he developed severe bifrontal throbbing headaches with nausea and vomiting. Two days prior, he was evaluated at an outside emergency department, tested positive for adenovirus, and was discharged after supportive treatment without symptom relief.

His oncology history included stage III prostate adenocarcinoma treated with prostatectomy and radiation in 2013, followed by detection of bilateral lung nodules and sclerotic bone lesions in 2016, and a 2020 biopsy of a left upper lobe lesion confirming mismatch repair deficient, androgen receptor–positive metastatic prostate cancer treated with enzalutamide, then abiraterone acetate and prednisone, and palliative radiation.

On presentation, vital signs were: temperature 37°C, heart rate 90 beats/min, blood pressure 164/81 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Neurologic examination revealed no focal motor or sensory deficits; intact coordination on dysdiadochokinesia, finger-to-nose, and heel-to-shin testing; an intact gait despite dizziness; and a positive right-sided Dix–Hallpike maneuver with horizontal nystagmus.

Noncontrast head CT showed a 3 cm left cerebellar hemispheric mass with surrounding vasogenic edema causing mild partial effacement of the fourth ventricle and left quadrigeminal cistern. The patient received dexamethasone. MRI of the brain demonstrated a cystic enhancing lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere with mass effect; no other intra-axial lesions were identified. Cerebral angiography revealed no abnormal hyperemia at the site of the lesion.

A hemangioblastoma was considered the leading diagnosis; other considerations included metastases and infarction.

His medical history included hypertension and treated tuberculosis; he was an ex–cigarette smoker. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests revealed a cytoplasmic ANCA titre of 1 / 20 and a PR3 level of 14.6 IU ml−1. The patient was started on subcutaneous methotrexate, and after 3 months a chest radiograph showed reduction of the nodule to 2 cm. He then developed renal impairment attributed to disease progression and/or methotrexate toxicity, and treatment was switched to high-dose intravenous cyclophosphamide with a tapering dose of oral prednisolone. A 75-year-old woman, previously well, transferred her care to a new general practitioner in June 2022. She reported a presumed stroke in April 2020 with slurred speech, imbalance, and confusion lasting 48 hours; at that time, brain MRI showed chronic periventricular white matter changes without acute ischemic lesions, and CT angiography demonstrated carotid tortuosity with stenosis from myointimal plaques. Her medications included barnidipine 20 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg daily.

Since 2020, she experienced recurrent dizzying attacks characterized by sudden subjective vertigo, absence of nausea or vomiting, and unsteadiness with a wide-based gait requiring support; episodes lasted days to weeks and gradually resolved. Symptomatic treatments for dizziness were ineffective. Over months, attacks increased in frequency and duration until dizziness became constant, leading to loss of autonomy.

At the first visit, general and neurologic examinations were normal, and she reported a low mood. Days later, a severe attack prevented her from getting out of bed, prompting a home visit. Vital signs were normal; she was alert, oriented, and cooperative with normal speech. She described severe dizziness worsened by any movement or position change, without nausea or vomiting. With assistance, she sat on the bed with difficulty maintaining trunk control. When upright, she adopted a wide-based stance, was unsteady, and required external supports to walk. Romberg’s test was positive, with marked unsteadiness on eye closure. Strength and sensation were intact, reflexes were normal, and cranial nerves were intact. The finger–nose test was weakly positive on the right. The HINTS examination was negative.

A diagnostic algorithm for dizziness suggested a low probability of central or peripheral vestibular origin. Review of the CTA suggested that carotid stenosis had been overestimated due to marked vessel tortuosity. Transcranial Doppler confirmed tortuosity and plaques but demonstrated normal hemodynamics of the cerebro-afferent vessels. Repeat brain MRI showed no signs of recent vascular lesions.

A 71-year-old woman with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and ischemic heart disease presented with a 2-month history of intermittent painless hematuria with passage of clots. She denied dysuria, frequency, or other lower urinary tract symptoms, and there was no family history of malignancy. On examination, vital signs and abdominal and pelvic exams were unremarkable. Laboratory evaluation showed a hemoglobin level of 8.6 g/dL requiring blood transfusion; serum creatinine and other biochemical parameters were within normal limits. Transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a 2.9 × 2.5 × 2.4 cm polypoidal mass arising from the posterolateral wall of the bladder dome; both kidneys and the upper tracts appeared normal. Pre- and postvoid bladder volumes were 180 mL and 44 mL, respectively. Cystoscopy demonstrated an exophytic solid tumor measuring 1.5 × 2.0 cm on the anterior fundal wall, covered with slough. A deep transurethral resection of the bladder tumor was performed. Histopathological analysis revealed an adenocarcinoma composed of mucinous and signet-ring cell components. Thus, a secondary adenocarcinoma or a rare variant of primary adenocarcinoma of the bladder was suspected.

A 48-year-old white man, a lifelong non-smoker with a remote bronchoscopic resection of a tracheal carcinoid 17 years earlier, presented with a three-month history of mild hemoptysis and cough without dyspnea. He also noted a non-tender, 2 × 2 cm subcutaneous mass on his left forearm without overlying skin changes. On examination, his vital signs were normal with an oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, and coagulation profile, were all within normal limits. A chest CT scan showed a polypoid lesion in the precarinal tracheal region adjacent to the anterior wall. Flexible bronchoscopy revealed a mass arising from the anterior tracheal wall just above the main carina, causing an 80% obstruction of the right main bronchus and 70% obstruction of the left main bronchus. The lesion was resected bronchoscopically with electrocautery, restoring full airway patency without complication. On hematoxylin–eosin staining, the tumor consisted of large nests of eosinophilic cells within a collagenous and myxoid matrix, and a carcinoid tumor was initially suspected.
